cover.headline: Rubber has squeezed the margin; at 18x Sep-28E EPS the recovery is not in the price
cover.lead: MRF is India's largest tyre maker (~32% of units sold), with 69% of sales in the replacement market, no net debt and ~₹7,600 cr of cash and liquid funds. Q1FY27 revenue grew 9.6% but the EBITDA margin fell to 11.8% (13.9% a year earlier) as natural rubber rose to ~₹275/kg. We forecast EPS of ₹4,880 / ₹6,254 / ₹7,380 for FY27-29E: a dip, then recovery as price increases catch up. The street values MRF on **P/E on one-year-forward EPS** (MOSL 19x FY28E). The house rule (MRF's forward P/E median since 2021, 24.1x, cut by the 10.5% tyre-sector de-rating) gives **21.5x Sep-28E EPS of ₹6,817 = {{dcf.tp|inr}} ({{dcf.upside|chg}}): we initiate with BUY**, close to the 15% line. Cross-checks: EV/EBITDA ₹1,53,089, DCF ₹1,27,455. Bull case {{scen.bull.tp|inr}}; bear case {{scen.bear.tp|inr}}.

arguments.p: Unit share rose to 31.9% in FY26 (~30% in FY25, CARE); OEM demand was "buoyant" and replacement "robust" in Q1FY27 (MOSL). MRF sells through 5,000+ dealers and calls itself the "definitive market leader" in two-wheeler tyres (AR FY26). Revenue has grown 14% a year since FY21.

arguments.h: The margin is at a cyclical low, not a new normal
arguments.p: Raw material jumped to 67.3% of revenue in Q1 (61.7% in Q4FY26). The industry has taken 7-9% of price increases with more in Q2; CRISIL calls FY27 "a cost-pass-through lag rather than a structural profitability reset" and sees margins recover in FY28. MRF's margin was 10.4% in FY23 and 17.0% a year later.

arguments.h: But returns are mediocre and governance favours the family
arguments.p: ROE has been 10-13% in normal years and never above 13.3% since FY18; the payout is ~4%, so cash piles up at ~6%. The five executive directors (all Mammen family) were paid ₹157 cr in FY26, more than total dividends (~₹100 cr). A ₹622 cr CCI penalty is unprovided.

arguments.h: Valuation: cheap against its own history, not against cash flows
arguments.p: At ₹1,25,280 MRF trades at 20.0x FY28E and 18.4x Sep-28E EPS, below its 24.1x forward median and 22% below its Oct-2025 high. The DCF (₹1,27,455) says the price is about fair on cash flows, and the post-Q1 street median is ₹1,35,500. The upside needs the margin to recover to ~14% by FY28E.

catalysts: Q2FY27 results (due by mid-November 2026): the first full quarter of price increases against rubber at ~₹270-275/kg.
Natural rubber after Southeast Asia's seasonal peak tapping window; CRISIL's trigger is a level below ₹250/kg.
Further price increases in replacement and OEM pass-through clauses in H2FY27.
Monsoon outcome and rural demand (tractor and farm tyres); festive-season replacement demand.
Supreme Court hearing on the CCI penalty; AIS-142 phase 2 noise norms (H2FY27) shifting OEM trucks to radials.

sections.title: India's largest tyre maker: one in three tyres sold, seven in ten rupees from the replacement market

blocks.p: MRF (Madras Rubber Factory) makes tyres, tubes, flaps and tread rubber for every kind of vehicle: trucks and buses, two- and three-wheelers, cars and SUVs, light commercial vehicles, tractors, off-the-road machines and aircraft. It sold ~31.9% of all tyre units sold by Indian makers in FY26 (CARE), from nine plants with 99.41 mn tyres of capacity. It reports one segment. Three facts matter for the numbers. **Replacement** (tyres sold through 5,000+ dealers to vehicle owners) is 69.1% of sales, **OEM** (fitted on new vehicles, incl. defence) 23.3% and **exports** ~7.6%. **Truck and bus tyres** are about half of revenue (49% in FY25), two- and three-wheelers 19%, cars 13%. And **raw materials** (natural rubber, synthetic rubber, carbon black, nylon and steel cord) are ~60-67% of revenue, a third of them imported.

sections.title: Eighty years, one family, no splits: what shaped the numbers

blocks.p: MRF began in 1946 as a toy-balloon maker in Madras and is still run by the founder's family: K.M. Mammen (Chairman & MD) and Arun Mammen (Vice Chairman & MD), with the next generation on the board. It has never split its shares or issued bonus shares in the period we examined, so 42.4 lakh shares trade at ₹1.25 lakh each, which keeps retail ownership and liquidity low. Three things in the history change how to read the numbers: the move from a September to a March year (FY16 was 18 months long, so our model starts at FY17), the GST changeover in Jul-2017 (FY17-18 revenue includes excise duty), and a CCI cartel penalty that has been in court since 2018.

sections.title: Tyres in FY27: demand holds, costs jump 35-40%, margins fall ~200-250bp before they recover

blocks.p: Indian tyre industry revenue ~₹1.36 lakh cr in FY26; the top six makers are ~85% of it (CRISIL, 24-Aug-2026). Tyre industry grew an estimated 10% in FY26 and tyre exports 9% (MRF AR FY26 MD&A); CRISIL: volume +7-8%, operating margin ~14.2%. For FY27 the picture changed with the Middle East conflict and a poor rubber season. CRISIL (24-Aug-2026) expects volume growth to slow to 4-5%, key input costs to rise 35-40% (natural rubber ~₹275/kg in June against ~₹220/kg in FY26) and the industry's operating margin to fall 200-250bp to ~11.5-12%, recovering to 13-13.5% in FY28 if input costs stabilise.

blocks.callout: **Our read:** the industry has done this before. In FY22-23 rubber and crude rose and MRF's margin fell to ~10%; in FY24 costs eased and it jumped to 17%. CRISIL calls FY27 "a cost-pass-through lag rather than a structural profitability reset". We agree, but the timing of the recovery depends on rubber, which nobody can forecast well, and on whether new capacity lets one of the big four break ranks on price.

blocks.callout: **Verdict:** the demand tailwind is real and MRF, as the largest player with the biggest dealer network, takes its share of it (31.9% of units, up from ~30%). But the tailwind arrives as revenue. Whether it becomes profit depends on the rubber-to-price spread, and in FY27 that spread is moving against the whole industry.

sections.title: Replacement pays the bills; OEM brings volume; exports have stalled

blocks.p: MRF does not report revenue by channel or product; CARE publishes the rounded mix each September. **Replacement** (69.1% of FY26 sales) is the profit centre: prices are set by the tyre makers, move first when costs rise, and demand follows the vehicle parc and freight activity rather than new-vehicle sales. In FY25 replacement volume grew only 5% (revenue +9%), while **OEM** volume grew 15% (revenue +19%) and **exports** 22% (revenue +23%) (CARE). In FY26 OEM gained share (23.3% from 22.1%) as GST 2.0 lifted vehicle sales; exports were flat at ₹2,324 cr as the Philippines, Bangladesh and the Middle East weakened (AR FY26).

blocks.callout: **Why the mix matters:** a rupee of replacement revenue earns more than a rupee of OEM revenue (CARE calls replacement "margin-accretive"; OEM prices catch up with costs only through periodic pass-through, CLSA), so the OEM share rising from 21% to 23% over two years has quietly diluted margins even before rubber. Exports should be MRF's growth option but have stalled; Apollo (Europe) and BKT (off-highway) are the Indian names with real global franchises, not MRF.

sections.title: The margin is a rubber spread: Q1FY27 gross margin fell 566bp in one quarter

blocks.p: Raw materials were 61.7% of standalone revenue in Q4FY26 and 67.3% in Q1FY27 (MOSL), a 5.6pp jump in one quarter. Natural rubber, about half of the raw-material bill, rose from ~₹220/kg (FY26 average) to ~₹275/kg in June 2026 (CRISIL) and was still ~₹273/kg on 3-Sep-2026; crude-linked inputs rose with the Middle East conflict. MRF raised prices, but the industry's 7-9% increases cover only part of a 35-40% rise in inputs. The consolidated EBITDA margin fell to 11.77% (Q1FY26 13.95%; Q4FY26 16.2%). MRF discloses no rubber hedging and says little beyond "margins are likely to be impacted on account of higher commodity prices and transport costs" (AR FY26 outlook).

blocks.title: Moat scorecard
blocks.source: GAM research compilation (AR FY26, CARE Ratings, CRISIL, broker notes to Aug-2026)

blocks.callout: **Honest verdict:** MRF has a real but narrow moat. Its brand, its 5,000-dealer replacement network and its scale in truck and two-wheeler tyres protect market share (~32% of units, rising). They do not protect margins: MRF buys the same rubber and crude derivatives as Apollo, CEAT and JK, at the same prices, and its EBITDA margin has moved with theirs for a decade. Returns on equity of 10-13% in normal years say the moat is worth share, not super-normal profit.

sections.title: Revenue doubled in seven years; profit follows the rubber price, not the volume

blocks.p: MRF's revenue was ₹16,062 cr in FY19 and ₹31,149 cr in FY26: 9.9% a year, and 14.0% a year since FY21 as vehicle sales recovered and tyre prices rose. Profit did not follow a line. The EBITDA margin swung from 18.3% in FY21 to 10.4% in FY23, back to 17.0% in FY24 and 15.8% in FY26, almost entirely on the cost of natural rubber and crude-linked inputs (carbon black, synthetic rubber, nylon cord), which take 60-67% of revenue. EPS went from ₹3,011 (FY21) to ₹1,578 (FY22), ₹4,907 (FY24) and ₹5,720 (FY26). The FY17-18 revenue figures are distorted by the change from excise duty to GST (Jul-2017), so we use FY19 as the start of growth comparisons.

pair.title: Revenue: ₹16,062 cr (FY19) to ₹31,149 cr (FY26)
Net profit: the FY22-23 rubber squeeze halved it, FY24-26 tripled it
EBITDA margin: 10% to 20% depending on raw materials
Raw materials: 56-67% of revenue

blocks.callout: **Our view:** MRF is a very large, well-run converter of rubber into tyres, and its profit is a spread: tyre prices minus rubber and crude. Over ten years the spread averaged ~15% of revenue (median FY17-26: 15.0%), but it has been above 17% or below 11% in four of those ten years. The volume engine is reliable; the margin is not. That is why its earnings, and the P/E the market pays, move in wide cycles.

bullets: **Demand was good.** OEM demand was "buoyant" as vehicle sales grew across segments and replacement "continued to be robust" (MOSL). Revenue grew 9.6% with only part of the price increases in.
**Costs were not.** Raw material jumped to 67.3% of revenue (63.4% in FY26); gross margin fell 566bp quarter on quarter (Moneycontrol). Price increases and cost measures only partly offset it.

**Other income carried the profit.** ₹195 cr against ₹129 cr a year earlier (MOSL had expected ₹140 cr), mostly treasury gains on a larger cash pile; without the ₹66 cr increase, net profit would have fallen ~11% instead of ~1%.

**Outlook (as known on 30-Sep-2026).** MRF holds no calls; MOSL reports management "cautious" on demand given the risk of a sub-normal monsoon, with raw material firm on the Middle East conflict. The AR FY26 says margins "are likely to be impacted". CARE (28-Sep-2026) expects pricing actions and cost control to support "a gradual recovery in margins". Q2FY27 results are due by mid-November 2026.

sections.title: Heavy capex, a 4% payout and a growing cash pile: returns of 10-13% on equity

blocks.p: Tyres need capital. MRF spent ₹18,410 cr on capex over FY17-26 (₹8,505 cr in FY17-21 and ₹9,905 cr in FY22-26), close to its ₹24,153 cr of operating cash flow, and lifted capacity to 99.4 mn tyres (CARE). Capex peaked at ₹3,291 cr in FY23 and slowed to ₹1,309-1,434 cr in FY25-26, so free cash flow jumped to ₹3,164 cr in FY26. Dividends were only ₹567 cr in ten years: MRF pays ₹200-235 a share, ~4% of profit. The rest stayed in the company, so net worth grew from ₹8,641 cr to ₹20,974 cr, and cash and liquid investments reached ₹7,572 cr (CARE, Mar-26). The result is modest returns: ROE of 10-13% in normal years, 5% in the FY22-23 trough, never above 13.3% since FY18.

blocks.callout: **The capital question:** MRF keeps reinvesting at returns close to its cost of equity (~12%) and lets the rest pile up in debt funds and deposits that earn ~6% before tax. A higher payout or a buyback would lift ROE; the family has shown no interest in either, and the board pays its five executive directors (all family) more than all shareholders together receive in dividends. Capex is now rising again: capital commitments doubled to ₹1,514 cr at Mar-26.

sections.title: Earnings quality: clean and conservative, but treasury income will be a fifth of pre-tax profit in FY27E

bullets: **Cash conversion is good over a cycle.** Cash from operations was 189% of net profit in FY26 (₹4,590 cr) and 100% in FY25, when inventory rose ₹1,156 cr. Over FY17-26 operating cash (₹24,153 cr) was 1.7x net profit (₹14,267 cr). Working capital swings with rubber stocking: FY22 operating cash was negative.
**Few one-offs.** Exceptional items: ₹63 cr in FY26 (labour codes); nothing material in FY24-25. Screener nets the FY26 charge into other income (₹440 cr vs ₹505 cr reported).

**Treasury income is growing and partly mark-to-market.** FY26 other income of ₹505 cr included ₹223 cr of fair-value gains on debt and arbitrage mutual funds (₹97.5 cr of it unrealised, per the cash flow statement), ₹170 cr of interest and ₹27 cr of insurance claims (one-off). It was 16% of profit before tax. We forecast ₹{{F.otherIncome.0|num}} cr in FY27E (twelve months to Jun-26: ₹571 cr before the labour-code charge), 6.3% on average gross treasury plus ~₹82 cr of export incentives, grant unwinding and sundry income.

**Conservative on provisions, but one big item is off the books.** The ₹622 cr CCI penalty is disclosed, not provided. EPR costs for waste tyres (₹150 cr in FY26, +24%) are a new, growing charge that peers also bear.
**Pay is a real cost.** Directors' remuneration of ₹157 cr in FY26 (incl. ₹93 cr of commission payable) is 6.5% of net profit, and it now rises with profit.

blocks.callout: **Accounting flag: GREEN.** Joint statutory auditors, unqualified opinion, simple structure (one business, small subsidiaries), no acquisitions or capitalised development costs, and little use of exceptional items. Two things to watch: mark-to-market fund gains inside other income, and the unprovided CCI penalty.

sections.title: Net cash of ~₹4,400 cr after leases; working capital is the swing item

blocks.p: At Mar-2026 MRF held ₹3,057 cr of debt and arbitrage mutual funds, ₹323 cr of bonds, ₹3,880 cr of bank deposits (₹2,013 cr of them longer than a year, which Screener counts in other assets), ₹305 cr of cash and ₹18 cr of listed shares: ₹7,582 cr gross. Against that it owed ₹2,367 cr to banks (mostly working-capital loans repayable on demand) and ₹840 cr of leases: net cash ~₹5,215 cr before leases, ~₹4,376 cr after (₹10,300 a share). CARE counts dealer deposits and supplier acceptances as debt too and puts net cash at ₹1,462 cr. Working capital is large: inventory of ~100-120 days of cost, partly rubber bought ahead; receivables ~42 days; payables only ~60 days. The engine's "treasury" is net of borrowings and leases in forecast years.

sections.title: Ownership: Mammen family 27.8%, foreign funds 17%, Indian institutions 12%

blocks.p: The Mammen family and its companies own 27.77% (Jun-2026): Comprehensive Investment and Finance Co 10.42%, Peninsular Investments 2.93%, individual family members 11.53% and other family companies (incl. The Malayala Manorama Co) ~2.9%; 0.09% is pledged. Foreign portfolio investors own 17.43%, mutual funds 7.08%, insurers 3.38%. The largest non-promoter holder is the Mowi Foundation (11.98%); Evertrue Charitable & Educational Foundation (2.99%) and Enam Securities (2.59%) follow. With 68,876 shareholders and a price of ₹1.25 lakh a share, MRF is one of the least-traded large Indian stocks.

blocks.p: Revenue comes from the channel build (replacement, OEM, exports; chapter above). The EBITDA margin is our call on the rubber spread ({{F.ebitdaMargin.0|pct}} / {{F.ebitdaMargin.1|pct}} / {{F.ebitdaMargin.2|pct}}). Capex is ₹2,000-2,200 cr a year (commitments doubled to ₹1,514 cr); depreciation 7.4% of gross block. Other income is built: 6.2% on average gross treasury (FY26 actual) plus ~₹82 cr of recurring non-treasury items. Interest ₹360-370 cr; tax 25%; payout 4.5%. Every assumption, with our reasoning, is in the Excel model's Assumptions sheet.

sections.title: The street after Q1: two Sells, two Buys; targets ₹1.14-1.65 lakh, median ₹1,35,500

blocks.p: Coverage of MRF is thin and split. After the Q1FY27 results (11-Aug-2026) Motilal Oswal kept Sell with ₹1,13,936 (19x FY28E EPS of ₹5,997), calling 25.5x/21.9x FY27E/FY28E "expensive" for ~10% returns; Kotak Securities kept Sell with ₹1,25,000 on commodity headwinds and industry-like growth; Axis Capital raised its Buy target to ₹1,46,000; CLSA stayed Outperform with ₹1,65,240, expecting margins to recover on price increases. Median of the four: ₹1,35,500, +8% vs the 30-Sep-2026 close of ₹1,25,280. The only house whose method we can see uses **P/E on one-year-forward EPS** (MOSL: 19x FY28E in August, 20x Dec-27E in February). The debate is not about demand; it is about how fast the rubber spread recovers and what multiple ~10-12% ROE deserves.

sections.title: Our honest summary: a margin trough in India's best tyre franchise, at a fair-to-cheap multiple; BUY, but only just

blocks.callout: **What you are buying:** India's largest tyre maker (~32% of units, rising), with the strongest replacement brand and dealer network, no net debt and ~₹7,600 cr of cash and liquid investments. Its profit is a spread between tyre prices and rubber and crude, and that spread is at a cyclical low: Q1FY27 EBITDA margin 11.8% against a ten-year median of 15.0%.

**What you are paying:** 20.0x our FY28E and 18.4x Sep-28E EPS. Since 2021 the market has paid a median 24.1x one-year-forward for MRF; tyre stocks were 10.5% below their five-year medians on 30-Sep-2026. On the street's method and the house multiple (21.5x) the target is {{dcf.tp|inr}} ({{dcf.upside|chg}}): BUY. The upside is close to the 15% line, the DCF (₹1,27,455) says the price is about fair on cash flows, and a history window without FY22-23 would give HOLD. This is a "margins recover on schedule" call, with low returns on capital as the main argument against.

bullets: **Rating: BUY, target {{dcf.tp|inr}} ({{dcf.upside|chg}}).** Our ratings follow the upside to our 12−month target: BUY at +15% or more, HOLD between −5% and +15%, SELL below −5%.
**The rule flips to HOLD above ~₹1,27,450** (a ~2% rise from ₹1,25,280) and to SELL above ~₹1,54,280, on today's numbers.

**This is an earnings-recovery call.** We assume the margin climbs from 11.8% (Q1) to {{F.ebitdaMargin.1|pct}} in FY28E. If it stays at ~12.5%, FY28E EPS falls ~₹987 and the target falls to ~₹1,25,340, about today's price.

**Against the street:** our target is above the post-Q1 median (₹1,35,500) because our Sep-28E EPS (₹6,817) includes a margin recovery that MOSL and Kotak do not yet assume, and because the house multiple (21.5x) is above MOSL's 19x. At 19x our target would be ~₹1,29,520.
**Biggest swing factor:** the rubber spread, then the multiple. Each 1x is ~₹6,817 a share.
